sections.label: The opening
sections.line: On 11 November 2016 I gave the keynote at…
sections.para: On 11 November 2016 I gave the keynote at BSidesLisbon, Hacking Portugal and making it a global player in software development, 103 slides, and three weeks later published it as a book on Leanpub, 75 pages, which still says 95% complete.

sections.label: In short
sections.para: November 2016, Lisbon. The BSidesLisbon keynote, 103 slides, then a book. The book is still at 95%. Published 1 December 2016, never finished. Hack Portugal. Hostile to insecure code; a Hacking Service; a league like football. Code as a national asset. Made in Portugal, OpenSource.pt, a Ministry of Code. Europe brought the regulation. The Clear Software Act, more or less.

sections.label: The talk and the book
sections.line: I gave Hacking Portugal as the keynote at BSidesLisbon…
sections.para: I gave Hacking Portugal as the keynote at BSidesLisbon on 11 November 2016; the video is 49 minutes.

sections.label: Hostile to insecure code
sections.line: The talk opened with a Portuguese network "to be…
sections.para: The talk opened with a Portuguese network "to be hostile to insecure code": make it hard to create, publish or host insecure apps and devices in Portugal, by regulation, by market pressure and by a community that attacks vulnerable code before criminals do.

sections.label: A Hacking Service, and hacking like football
sections.line: The idea people remember was the Portuguese Hacking Service…
sections.para: The idea people remember was the Portuguese Hacking Service : update the old compulsory military service into a hacking service for 15 to 21 year olds, to "hack everything that is plugged-in to Portugal's network", code-review open-source and strategic code, contribute fixes, and "help SMEs with their digital security and DevOps", paid for by moving a share of the military budget to cyber.

sections.label: Code as a national asset
sections.line: The second half was about code as something a…
sections.para: The second half was about code as something a country owns.

sections.label: Why Portugal, then and now
sections.line: The talk ended with a choice: Portugal could "be…
sections.para: The talk ended with a choice: Portugal could "be a garden for Europe, a holiday destination", or "a powerhouse that inspires and leads the world in technology and secure coding", working with the Portuguese-speaking countries. The book's last chapter argued it is easier in a small country, "more likely to have fewer agendas and fewer lobby groups wielding influence".

sections.label: What a new edition needs
sections.line: A new edition of Hacking Portugal, for Web Summit…
sections.para: A new edition of Hacking Portugal, for Web Summit in November, would keep the structure and change the centre of gravity: from application security to agents, language and sovereignty.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: "As far as I know" means I did not…
sections.para: "As far as I know" means I did not survey it. Some of these ideas may exist in a form I missed. The Clear Software Act is an analogy. The CRA is the EU's law, not mine. The commentary is mine, now. The slides are from 2016, unchanged.
